value_chain_position: Power-management and connectivity component maker - sells connectors, power-distribution components and sensors into grid power distribution, data-center build-out and vehicle electrification (the chain's power-management and connectors layer). The data-provider 'Semiconductors' classification is a filing quirk, not the real business.
cost_curve_verified: No output commodity here, so the equivalent test is input cost against gross margin: our screen's 19% free-cash-flow margin and 15.5% revenue growth both agree with the company's reported figures (trailing free cash flow $3.64B on $19.15B of revenue; fiscal-2026 guidance of roughly 15% sales growth), and the screen's 0.97 times net-debt-to-earnings reading agrees with the $4.39B of net debt reported at 26 June 2026 - but it will understate leverage to about 1.2 times once the $1.4B Astrodyne TDI purchase closes by year-end 2026.
gm_trajectory: Revenue grew 14% year over year in the June-2026 quarter with gross margin at 35.6% versus 35.3% a year earlier, so margin is expanding on growing revenue - but it has compressed from 37.2% in the December-2025 quarter as zero-margin copper pass-through pricing entered the mix; the operating line is the cleaner read and it expanded 90 basis points year over year to 22.0%, with Industrial Solutions at 22.8% and Transportation Solutions at 21.0%. Our screen's 'expanding' label agrees on the multi-year and year-over-year view and disagrees with the last two quarters.
bull_thesis:
TE Connectivity is a component manufacturer that has quietly become the second-largest supplier of the connectors and power hardware that artificial-intelligence data centers and modernised electricity grids cannot be built without - and it is priced as though it were still mainly a car-parts company. That gap is the whole case.

Start with the demand evidence, which is unusually hard for a technology story. Orders - the leading indicator, since they are placed before revenue is recognised - have risen for five consecutive quarters, from $4.5 billion in the June-2025 quarter to a record $5.7 billion in the June-2026 quarter, up 27% year over year, with double-digit growth in every single business and every region. The book-to-bill ratio (orders divided by sales) is 1.1 both in the quarter and year-to-date, meaning the company is taking in more work than it is shipping, and management states plainly that this has produced a record backlog giving visibility into fiscal 2027. Digital Data Networks orders are up over 70% year-to-date. This is not a projection; it is signed demand already on the books.

The artificial-intelligence business has beaten its own public target early. Revenue from these applications went from $300 million in fiscal 2024 to over $900 million in fiscal 2025, and by the June-2026 quarter the company had reached the $3 billion annual run rate it laid out at its November-2025 investor day - ahead of schedule. Terrence Curtin, the chief executive, in July 2026: 'the $3 billion we laid out, we're ahead of, and that has continued to shift left.' Importantly, about one-third of that revenue is power connectivity rather than data connectivity, and power content rises as rack architectures move toward 800 volts.

The second engine is the electricity grid. The energy business grew 33% organically in the June-2026 quarter on utilities replacing ageing infrastructure and on the power build-out feeding data centers. The $2.3 billion Richards Manufacturing purchase completed in fiscal 2025 bought a leading position in North American underground distribution equipment, and management says it is running ahead of the original plan.

Profitability is improving while all this happens, which is the real test. Adjusted operating margin rose from 20.0% to 22.0% year over year. Industrial Solutions margins expanded by roughly 400, 300 and 500 basis points in three of the last four quarters to reach 22.8%. Heath Mitts, the chief financial officer, has promised 'roughly 30% flow-through' - meaning thirty cents of every incremental sales dollar reaches operating profit - on every single call, has been challenged on it by analysts repeatedly, and delivered about 36% in the June-2026 quarter.

The moat claim is specific rather than generic. Connectors are designed into a customer's architecture years before volume, so displacing an incumbent means requalifying the platform. Curtin on 800-volt data centers, July 2026: 'I don't see new entrants coming in because this is a simultaneous equation of trade-offs and constraints between the data and the power equation when you're at the rack.' Corroborating evidence from outside the company: reports of coordinated connector price increases of 5% to 15% from TE Connectivity, Amphenol and Molex effective July 2026 - that is a concentrated market exercising pricing power, not a commodity market.

Management has earned trust the hard way. It guided and beat both sales and adjusted earnings per share in four consecutive quarters (guided $4.55B/$2.27 and delivered $4.75B/$2.44; guided $4.5B/$2.53 and delivered $4.67B/$2.72; guided $4.7B/$2.65 and delivered $4.74B/$2.73; guided $5.0B/$2.83 and delivered $5.16B/$2.94). Cash conversion has run above 100%, free cash flow was over $3 billion in fiscal 2025, roughly all of it is returned to shareholders, the dividend was raised 10% in March 2026, and diluted share count has fallen from 305 million to 293 million in seven quarters. Net debt is $4.39 billion against roughly $4.85 billion of trailing operating cash earnings - under one times.

The re-rating mechanism is the mix. In the June-2026 quarter Industrial Solutions and Transportation Solutions each printed exactly $2.58 billion of sales - the first time they have been equal. Industrial grew 21.9%, Transportation 6.7%. The market has valued this company at a wide discount to Amphenol and Hubbell because more than half of it was automotive; from here, more than half of it is not. If the multiple simply migrates part-way toward the peer group as that becomes undeniable, the shares work without a single new assumption about demand.

Conditions that must hold: hyperscaler capital spending does not pause through fiscal 2027; copper cost increases continue to be passed through within a quarter or two; global auto production holds near the guided 88 million units; and the $1.4 billion Astrodyne TDI purchase integrates as cleanly as Richards did.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that this is a bad company - it plainly is not - but that you are being asked to pay a full price for peak conditions in a business whose two growth engines share one customer, at a moment when its main raw material is at an all-time high.

First, the concentration is worse than the segment chart suggests. Digital Data Networks and the energy business are both now explicitly levered to the same demand: data-center construction. Management said so in July 2026 - 'Our AI opportunity extends beyond the rack. Data center build-outs are driving significant investment across the power infrastructure.' Curtin has been equally clear about who the buyer is: 'the bigger driver of growth for us is the hyperscalers that have their custom TPUs and GPUs.' Combined, these two businesses generated well over $1 billion of the quarter's $2.58 billion of Industrial revenue and essentially all of the growth. A digestion pause by a handful of buyers - not a collapse, just a pause - removes the entire growth story at once. Order books do not protect you here: orders can be rescheduled, and a record backlog built during a capital-spending boom is exactly the backlog that gets pushed out.

Second, copper. TE Connectivity is a connector maker; copper is a cost, not a revenue tailwind, and it hit roughly $14,000 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange on 4 August 2026 - a record. Management admits feeling it (January 2026: 'as the spot market goes up, we feel that... yes, we're feeling it right now') and passes it through, but pass-through revenue carries no profit. The proof is already in the accounts: gross margin has fallen from 37.2% in the December-2025 quarter to 36.8% and then 35.6% - about 1.6 percentage points of compression in two quarters while revenue grew. If copper stays here and the pass-through lags by even one quarter in a slowing order environment, the 30%-plus flow-through promise breaks, and that promise is load-bearing for the entire earnings model.

Third, the optical displacement risk is real and now conceded. Pressed for three consecutive quarters, Curtin finally said it plainly in July 2026: 'we are not a major player in scale-out. When you think about scale-out, which is almost all optical today, we have a limited position there.' Roughly two-thirds of the artificial-intelligence revenue is data connectivity - copper. The RAM Photonics purchase in April 2026 is a foothold, not a position. If scale-up networking inside the rack follows scale-out toward optical faster than management expects, the fastest-growing part of this company is displaced by a technology it does not lead. TE Connectivity is also the acknowledged number two: an analyst put a competitor at roughly three times its artificial-intelligence revenue in October 2025 and management did not dispute the figure.

Fourth, capital allocation is leaking value at the margin. The company has committed close to $4 billion to acquisitions in two years - $2.3 billion for Richards Manufacturing (about 5.8 times its roughly $400 million of sales) and $1.4 billion for Astrodyne TDI announced 22 July 2026 (about 5.6 times its 'more than $250 million' of sales). On the mid-30% cash margins management guided to for Richards, both were struck at roughly 16 to 17 times operating cash earnings - while TE Connectivity's own shares trade at about 14 times. Buying other companies for more than the market charges for your own is only accretive if synergies are quantified, and on five calls they never were. The market registered its objection: the shares fell 6.9% on 22 July 2026, the day of a beat on both lines with record orders, and the decline was attributed to the Astrodyne announcement rather than the results.

Fifth, the automotive half is not a source of support. Global auto production is guided at roughly 88 million units, 'down slightly,' with Western regions declining every quarter for over a year and growth carried entirely by Asia. Transportation Solutions grew 6.7% in the June-2026 quarter against Industrial's 21.9%. In a genuine recession this half of the company shrinks, and it is still half.

Sixth, the multiple is not a floor. The peer group - Amphenol at roughly 24 times enterprise value to operating cash earnings, Hubbell at 21 times, Eaton at 32 times - is at cycle-peak valuations on the same artificial-intelligence enthusiasm. A capital-spending scare de-rates the whole complex together, and TE Connectivity's discount does not exempt it. There is no structural floor under the shares: this is a company with net debt, not net cash, no deal terms, and no asset backing that supports a liquidation value anywhere near the market price. Tangible asset value is roughly $3.9 billion against a $62.6 billion market capitalisation.

What priced downside looks like: fiscal-2027 Industrial revenue of about $9.8 billion (a mid-single-digit decline as artificial-intelligence orders digest) at a 19.5% operating margin, and Transportation revenue of about $9.3 billion (down about 10% on an auto recession) at a 17.5% margin, gives roughly $3.4 billion of combined operating profit and about $8.95 of adjusted earnings per share. At 14 to 16 times - the multiple this company carried in the 2022-2023 industrial de-rating - that is $125 to $143 per share, or a fall of roughly 35% to 42% from $215.87. Confirmation would be a single quarter of book-to-bill below 1.0 in Industrial, or gross margin printing below 35% while copper is flat.
sop_bull:
$286 per share. Valuing each segment on the fiscal-2027 earnings the record backlog supports, and on multiples closer to what the market already pays comparable businesses.

- Industrial Solutions: revenue of about $12.0 billion (from a $10.3 billion run rate, growing on Digital Data Networks orders up over 70% year-to-date, energy up 33% organically, plus roughly $250 million from Astrodyne TDI), at a 24% adjusted operating margin as volume leverage continues, giving about $2.88 billion of operating profit and roughly $3.17 billion of operating cash earnings after adding back depreciation. At 20 times - still a discount to Amphenol's 24 times - that is $63.4 billion, or about $219 per share.
- Transportation Solutions: revenue of about $10.6 billion at a 21% margin, giving roughly $2.63 billion of operating cash earnings. At 9.5 times, reflecting best-in-class margins for a vehicle supplier and content growth of 4 to 6 points above market, that is $25.0 billion, or about $86 per share.
- Less pro-forma net debt of about $5.5 billion after the Astrodyne purchase closes: minus $19 per share.

Total about $286 per share. This requires no new demand assumption beyond the backlog already signed - only that the market stops valuing the company on its shrinking automotive half.
sop_bear:
$124 per share, assuming the chain regime turns against it: an artificial-intelligence capital-spending digestion, an auto recession, record copper compressing the pass-through, and a de-rating of the whole connector complex together.

- Industrial Solutions: revenue of about $9.8 billion (down mid-single digits as Digital Data Networks orders are rescheduled off a peak and energy slows), at a 19.5% operating margin as copper pass-through and under-absorbed new capacity bite, giving about $1.91 billion of operating profit and roughly $2.31 billion of operating cash earnings. At 12 times - where the group traded in the 2022-2023 industrial de-rating - that is $27.7 billion, or about $96 per share.
- Transportation Solutions: revenue of about $9.3 billion (global auto production down roughly 10% toward 80 million units), at a 17.5% margin, giving roughly $2.03 billion of operating cash earnings. At 7 times, a standard trough multiple for a vehicle supplier, that is $14.2 billion, or about $49 per share.
- Less net debt of about $6.0 billion, higher than today because the $1.4 billion Astrodyne purchase closes into a weaker cash-flow year: minus $21 per share.

Total about $124 per share. The company remains solidly solvent throughout - net debt would still be under 1.4 times operating cash earnings and free cash flow stays positive - so this is a de-rating, not an impairment, and continued buybacks at depressed prices provide a modest cushion above the arithmetic.
sop_breakdown:
Base case, valuing the two segments on the fiscal-2027 earnings the current backlog and guidance support, roughly eighteen months out:

- Industrial Solutions (artificial-intelligence interconnect, grid and energy, aerospace and defence, factory automation, medical): revenue of about $11.8 billion at a 23.5% adjusted operating margin gives roughly $2.77 billion of operating profit, or about $3.17 billion of operating cash earnings after depreciation. Valued at 17 times - a deliberate discount to Hubbell at 21 times and Amphenol at 24 times, because only about half of this segment is artificial-intelligence-driven - that is $53.9 billion, or about $186 per share.
- Transportation Solutions (automotive connectors and sensors, commercial vehicle): revenue of about $10.6 billion at a 21% margin gives roughly $2.23 billion of operating profit, or about $2.63 billion of operating cash earnings. Valued at 8.5 times, a premium to a typical vehicle supplier at 6 to 8 times because this business held above 20% margins through a declining Western auto market, that is $22.4 billion, or about $77 per share.
- Less pro-forma net debt of about $5.5 billion (the reported $4.39 billion at 26 June 2026 plus the $1.4 billion Astrodyne TDI purchase, partly offset by retained cash flow): minus $19 per share.

Total about $244 per share on roughly 290 million diluted shares. Cross-checked against earnings, this implies about 18.4 times a fiscal-2027 adjusted figure near $13.30 per share - demanding but not heroic for a business compounding earnings above 20% with a record backlog, and still a wide discount to how the market prices its closest comparable companies today.
risk_reward: At $215.87 the reward is thin and the risk is not. Our adverse case sits at $135 per share and our base-case fair value at $244, with the favourable case at $286. In other words, the shares are close enough to fair value that most of the identified upside is already in the price, while the adverse case - a pause in data-center spending, an auto downturn and record copper compressing the pass-through, all of which would arrive together - remains a long way below. The asymmetry only becomes attractive in the region of $190, which is both the 52-week low and roughly where the shares traded on 23 July 2026 immediately after the Astrodyne-driven sell-off; at that level the same $135 downside and $244 fair value produce a balanced trade, and below about $180 it turns clearly favourable. There is no structural floor to lean on: the company carries net debt of $4.39 billion rather than net cash, there are no deal terms, and tangible asset value of roughly $3.9 billion is immaterial against a $62.6 billion market capitalisation.
catalyst_status_note: There is no binding, dated event driving this name - which in this lane is neither a plus nor a penalty. What exists is a soft, non-binding set of developments: the record $5.7 billion order book and record backlog reported on 22 July 2026, which management ties to fiscal-2027 visibility but attaches no dated contractual payout to; the $1.4 billion Astrodyne TDI acquisition signed 22 July 2026 and expected to close by the end of calendar 2026, subject to regulatory clearance (a real dated corporate event, but a bolt-on adding only about $250 million of annual sales, roughly 1.3% of revenue); and the crossover of Industrial Solutions past Transportation Solutions in revenue, which happened in the June-2026 quarter ($2.58 billion each) and is a gradual re-rating argument rather than an event. The next scheduled disclosure is the fourth-quarter and full-year fiscal-2026 results, which the company has reported in late October in each of the last two years (29 October 2025 for the prior year), and which should carry the first formal fiscal-2027 outlook.
peer_comps_note:
The relative valuation is the core of the case and it is stark. On enterprise value to trailing operating cash earnings - the cleanest cross-company measure because it ignores capital structure - TE Connectivity trades at about 14.6 times as reported (closer to 13.8 times once a missing depreciation line in the June-2026 quarter is corrected), against Amphenol at 24.0 times, Hubbell at 21.4 times and Eaton at 31.8 times. On enterprise value to sales it is 3.50 times, against Amphenol at 7.76 times, Eaton at 6.41 times, Hubbell at 5.04 times and Littelfuse at 4.53 times. Littelfuse's earnings multiple is not usable - it is running a loss year and prints above 42 times. Belden and Rogers were not pulled in detail.

The discount is roughly 30% to Hubbell and 40% to Amphenol on operating cash earnings, and it has a legitimate explanation: just over half of TE Connectivity's revenue has been automotive, a business the market values at half the multiple of electrical infrastructure. What makes it interesting rather than merely explained is that the mix crossed over in the June-2026 quarter, with Industrial Solutions and Transportation Solutions each at exactly $2.58 billion of sales and Industrial growing at three times the rate. Our base-case multiples of 17 times for Industrial and 8.5 times for Transportation deliberately hold both below the peer set, so the fair value does not depend on the discount closing entirely. The offsetting caution: the comparison set itself is at cycle-peak valuations on artificial-intelligence enthusiasm, so anchoring to it in a downturn would flatter the answer.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is about what kind of company this is, not about how it is trading. Wall Street still prices TE Connectivity as an automotive supplier with an interesting side business. That classification expired in the June-2026 quarter, when Industrial Solutions and Transportation Solutions each printed exactly $2.58 billion of sales for the first time, with Industrial growing 21.9% against Transportation's 6.7%. From here the faster-growing, higher-margin half is the larger half, and it compounds the gap every quarter. The market has not repriced that: the shares change hands at roughly 14 times enterprise value to operating cash earnings against Hubbell at 21 times and Amphenol at 24 times, and they sit below their 200-day average price of about $220 even though adjusted earnings per share grew 22% in the latest quarter.

The second thing the street has wrong is what the 22 July 2026 sell-off meant. The shares fell 6.9% on a day the company beat on both sales and earnings, raised its outlook, reported record orders up 27% and reported a record backlog - and the decline was attributed to the simultaneous announcement of the $1.4 billion Astrodyne TDI acquisition. Investors reacted to the cheque, not to the business. We think the objection is legitimate in direction but overstated in size: Astrodyne is about 5.6 times its 'more than $250 million' of annual sales, essentially the same price paid for Richards Manufacturing in fiscal 2025, and Richards is running ahead of plan with the energy business growing 33% organically. Paying roughly 16 to 17 times for assets while your own shares trade at 14 times is a genuine value leak, but it applies to about $1.4 billion against a $62.6 billion market capitalisation.

The third disagreement is with the sell side's own arithmetic. The published price targets are stale and internally inconsistent: the consensus is $253 and the twelve-month average is $261, but the two freshest targets published on 23 July 2026 - immediately after the print - were $241 and $225, both set when the shares were near $198. Analysts cut their targets the day after a beat-and-raise with record orders. That is a group anchoring to the acquisition headline rather than to the order book.

Where we do not disagree with the market, and where we part company with the bull case: the price. Our reconstructed fair value of $244 is only about 13% above the current $215.87. The consensus target of $253 is not obviously wrong - it is roughly where our own work lands. This is a case of the market misunderstanding the character of the business while pricing the shares approximately correctly, which is an unsatisfying but honest conclusion.
valley_of_death:
The risky window over the next three to nine months is not about solvency - this company generates over $3 billion of free cash flow a year against $4.39 billion of net debt - it is about the collision of three things in the same two quarters.

First, copper. The price reached roughly $14,000 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange on 4 August 2026, an all-time high, driven by Chilean supply disruption and by demand from the very data centers TE Connectivity supplies. For a connector maker this is pure input inflation. The company recovers it through price, and the industry moved together on increases of 5% to 15% effective July 2026, but recovery revenue carries no profit attached. The damage is already visible: gross margin has fallen from 37.2% in the December-2025 quarter to 36.8% and then 35.6%, about 1.6 percentage points in two quarters while revenue grew. If the fourth-quarter print in late October shows gross margin below 35% while the operating margin holds only by cost cuts, the 'roughly 30% flow-through' promise that underpins every earnings model in the street comes into question.

Second, the Astrodyne TDI purchase closes by the end of calendar 2026 - $1.4 billion of cash out the door into a company that has been returning essentially 100% of its free cash flow to shareholders. Either the buyback pauses for two quarters or net debt rises toward 1.2 times operating cash earnings. Neither is dangerous; both are visible, and the market has already shown it will sell the stock over exactly this issue.

Third, and most important, the fourth-quarter report in late October carries the first formal fiscal-2027 guidance. Management has anchored expectations high - 'more than $2.5 billion of incremental revenue' this year, order growth of 27%, a record backlog, and a chief financial officer who said in July that 'as we jump into 2027, we would expect the same kind of momentum.' Anything less than double-digit growth guidance for fiscal 2027 will be read as the artificial-intelligence order book beginning to digest, and against a peer group priced for continued acceleration that reads badly for the whole complex.

The specific tell to watch: Industrial book-to-bill. It has run at 1.1 or better for four quarters. A single print below 1.0 in that segment, especially in Digital Data Networks where year-to-date orders are up over 70% against an easy base, converts a growth story into a peak-earnings argument overnight - and it will happen before any of it shows in reported revenue. Seasonality is a complication here: management warned in October 2025 that the December quarter naturally steps down because Western factories shut for holidays, so the reading needs to be taken against last year's comparable quarter rather than sequentially.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced-selling dynamic in this name, and that is worth saying clearly rather than manufacturing one. TE Connectivity pays a modest and rising dividend - raised 10% in the March-2026 quarter - so there is no income-focused shareholder base at risk of a cut, and no pivot in strategy that would breach an index or mandate rule. Trading is deep and orderly, with roughly $172 million of average daily dollar volume, so nothing about the shareholder register creates a mechanical liquidation.

What does exist is the reverse of a washout: crowding risk. The whole connector and electrical-equipment complex moved almost identically on 4 August 2026 - TE Connectivity up 5.3%, Amphenol up 5.0%, Hubbell up 4.9%, Belden up 4.8%, Rogers up 4.7% - which tells you these names are being traded as a single artificial-intelligence capital-spending basket rather than on company-specific merit. Correlated ownership of that kind cuts both ways, and it means TE Connectivity's valuation discount will not protect it in a sector-wide de-rating; it will simply de-rate from a lower starting point.

One modest observation on the register itself. Insider open-market activity offers no support: zero purchases against 37 sales totalling 115,317 shares. That is ordinary behaviour at a large company where executives are paid in stock and it is not evidence of a problem, but it is also not the buying you would expect if the people running the business believed the discount to peers were as unjustified as the bull case argues.

The practical implication for entry is the opposite of waiting for capitulation: the useful moments in this name have been single-stock dislocations, not market-wide ones. The shares fell 6.9% on 22 July 2026 on a beat-and-raise because the market disliked an acquisition. That is the kind of event that creates the entry level, and it lasted about a week.
forcing_function:
The event that would force a re-rating is the fourth-quarter and full-year fiscal-2026 report, which the company has delivered in late October in each of the last two years (29 October 2025 for the prior year; expect a similar date in 2026, with the announcement of the exact date typically issued about three weeks ahead). Two things land in that release.

The first is the fiscal-2027 outlook. Management has laid the ground carefully: a record $5.7 billion order book, a record backlog explicitly described as 'a strong growth indicator as we move into our fiscal 2027,' and the chief financial officer's July-2026 statement that 'as we jump into 2027, we would expect the same kind of momentum.' If that outlook lands at double-digit sales growth with adjusted earnings per share guided near or above $13, it validates the backlog and makes the current multiple visibly too low against a peer group paying 21 to 24 times. If it lands short, the peak-earnings argument wins and the multiple discount stops being an opportunity.

The second is the segment disclosure. Fiscal 2026 is the crossover year - Industrial Solutions and Transportation Solutions each printed $2.58 billion in the June quarter, and on full-year figures Industrial should reach roughly $9.9 billion against Transportation's roughly $9.9 billion. The first full year in which the company reports Industrial as its larger segment is the moment the automotive-supplier classification becomes indefensible in print rather than merely in argument. That is a slow catalyst, not a sharp one, and it is why this is a watchlist rather than an entry: the mechanism is real but it works over quarters.

A secondary dated item: the $1.4 billion Astrodyne TDI acquisition is expected to close by the end of calendar 2026 subject to regulatory clearance. Completion removes the uncertainty that knocked 6.9% off the shares on 22 July 2026, though the amount at stake is small relative to the company.

There is no activist angle here and no strategic process to anticipate. The sum-of-the-parts discount is real but it is a valuation discount on two well-run segments, not a conglomerate discount inviting a break-up: the two businesses share manufacturing footprint, materials science and customer engineering, and separating them would destroy more than it released.
moderator_conclusion:
This is an excellent business at an approximately fair price, and the discipline of this committee is to say so rather than to talk itself into the trade.

What the evidence establishes beyond argument: TE Connectivity is compounding revenue at about 15% with adjusted earnings per share up 22% in the June-2026 quarter, orders up 27% to a record $5.7 billion, a book-to-bill of 1.1 and a record backlog, operating margins expanding 90 basis points year over year to 22.0%, free cash flow of $3.64 billion over the last twelve months, net debt under one times operating cash earnings, and a management team that has guided and beaten both sales and earnings four quarters running while holding its chief financial officer's 'roughly 30% flow-through' promise under repeated analyst challenge. The forensic file is clean. The moat is wide and widening, evidenced by rising returns on capital and coordinated industry pricing rather than by assertion.

What the evidence also establishes: at $215.87 the shares are only about 13% below our reconstructed fair value of $244, while a coherent adverse case - a pause in data-center spending, an auto downturn toward 80 million units, and record copper at roughly $14,000 per tonne compressing a pass-through that has already cost 1.6 points of gross margin in two quarters - carries the shares to about $135. Those three risks are not independent; they arrive together. Accepting nearly 40% of downside for 13% of upside is not a decision this committee should make, however good the company is.

So the correct call is to wait, with a named level rather than a vague hope for weakness. The shares traded near $198 on 23 July 2026, the day after a beat-and-raise, because the market objected to a $1.4 billion acquisition; the 52-week low is $190. In the $185 to $195 region the same fair value and the same adverse case produce a balanced trade, and below roughly $180 the asymmetry turns clearly favourable. The alternative trigger is informational rather than price-based: if the fourth-quarter report in late October delivers a fiscal-2027 outlook at double-digit sales growth with adjusted earnings guided near $13 per share while gross margin stabilises above 35%, the peak-earnings objection is answered and paying up becomes defensible.

Two points of nuance worth carrying forward. First, the value case and the timing case genuinely diverge here, and we have scored them separately. On the business and the forensics alone this is close to the best-quality name in the electrification chain and it trades at a 30% to 40% discount to its closest comparable companies - that deserves a high value score. On entry timing, at a price this close to fair value with correlated risks live, it does not deserve a high conviction score. Second, do not be seduced by the relative-value argument in isolation: Amphenol at 24 times and Eaton at 32 times operating cash earnings are themselves priced for continued acceleration in artificial-intelligence capital spending. If that assumption breaks, the peer multiples fall toward TE Connectivity rather than the reverse, and the discount that looks like a margin of safety today would simply have been an accurate assessment of a more cyclical mix.

One last piece of honesty about the character of this position. Buying TE Connectivity is, to a greater degree than the two-segment reporting suggests, an underwriting of hyperscaler capital spending - Digital Data Networks and the energy business now share that single demand driver, and management said as much in July 2026. The automotive half is a stabiliser, not a diversifier, and it grew only 6.7%. Size accordingly if and when the price comes to you.
